snippet.textDisplay:
* Mars has low gravity, but it is not zero
	•	Mars’ gravity is about 38 %  of Earth’s gravity
	•	Gravity is produced by the total mass of the planet, not just its core
	•	Mars can capture gases, but not strongly or for long periods
	•	Mars has a very weak magnetic field
	•	Because of the weak magnetic field, solar wind gradually strips away the atmosphere
	•	Light gases such as hydrogen and helium escape first
	•	Mars still has an atmosphere, but it is very thin (about  only 1 %of Earth’s atmosphere)
	•	Due to the lack of a thick atmosphere, more solar radiation reaches the surface very  easily
       •     And it is absolutely impossible for humans to live in a dome for a long time.
	•	As a result, conditions on Mars are very harsh for life
	•	Humans on Earth breathe oxygen (O₂), but Mars has almost no free oxygen,
making human survival without life-support impossible.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@yk-649rvp This restrictive economic framework remained in place for almost five decades, from the 1950s through much of the 1980s in India.

A significant shift began in the 1990s under Manmohan Singh, then serving as Finance Minister, with political support from leaders such as P. V. Narasimha Rao. Further reforms and consolidation followed during the tenure of Atal Bihari Vajpayee. This period marked India’s decisive move toward liberalization, globalization, and privatization, dismantling much of the Licence Raj and opening the economy to broader competition and investment. For these reforms, Manmohan Singh is widely respected.

However, even during Man Mohan Singh cronyism and favoritism persisted in various sectors. Companies such as Kingfisher, led by Vijay Mallya, expanded during this period.

There have also been discussions in the public domain regarding the joint ventures of Mallya and Sharad Pawar, then senior minister in the UPA government. Questions have been raised about agricultural policy decisions, subsidy management, and the functioning of the Public Distribution System (PDS). Grains under PDS were being sold to Mallya at negligible cost. 

Similarly, misuse of public funds have been associated with leaders such as Lalu Prasad Yadav.

Before forming conclusions about India’s economic history, it is important to examine the broader context, the reforms undertaken, and the debates and criticisms that accompanied different political eras.

Unitree Robotics is one of the fastest moving companies in the robot world. Based in China, the company builds four legged robot dogs and full size humanoids that sprint across fields, climb stairs, and snap back to their feet almost instantly if someone shoves them. Watching them move feels less like looking at machines and more like watching trained athletes made of metal.

Inside, these robots are powered by compact electric motors that act like artificial muscles. That is how they pull off backflips, keep balance on rough ground, and adjust their posture in a split second. They constantly calculate their position in space, correcting themselves dozens of times every second.

One standout model is the G1 humanoid. snippet.textDisplay:
No. This is very clearly just a program running on a computer. All the steps are programed from the start. Their starting points are marked, the distance they have to travel calculated and programed so that every step is done according to instructions. These aren't Robots walking or doing backflips. This is a computer reading an instruction and sending signals to motors to imitate human behaviour. It's cool, but has little to no actual use outside cool acrobatics.

For something like Skynet you would need entirely different programs that can react and make decisions. We are nowhere close to that. Even AI like ChatGPT only follows a predefined program. It doesn't think, it just reads what you put in and then gives you a respone according to it's training, which is why it's so easily fooled or sometimes just makes stuff up. 

So don't worry, we won't see skynet for at least another 10 years. Probably.

Asimov 3 laws of robotics
Isaac Asimov, a pioneering science fiction writer, formulated the Three Laws of Robotics to govern the behavior of robots and ensure they act safely and ethically around humans. These laws have become foundational in discussions about artificial intelligence and robotics. Here they are:

A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.

A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law.

A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law.

Wang Xingxing is on record saying BD's current Atlas is far more advanced than anything he's built so far. What Unitree actually excels in is the open-source development model that lets them speed up the control aspects of their entire ecosystem compared to Hyundai-BD, as well as in bringing these robots to market to accelerate that open-source development. 

As more of these units get into the hands of people with brilliant ideas, those ideas eventually filter back to the company. You have to realize also that Atlas is limited by the complicated mechanics needed to make it such a generalist, forcing the weight to go up to 85 kg vs. a G1's 35 kg. G1s are less flexible but more capable in specific tasks.

Personally, I think Unitree's development model already won, but Wang himself thinks he still has a ways to go.

snippet.textDisplay:
Watching robots practice karate makes me think — instead of fearing robots replacing humans, why not train them for protection roles? Imagine deploying robots in public spaces that are specifically programmed to detect physical aggression, molestation attempts, or bullying. Not to replace judges or police, and not to deliver “instant justice,” but to act as neutral, fast-response protectors.
If a robot can identify aggressive movement, trigger alarms, record evidence, and physically intervene only to separate individuals (without excessive force), that alone could prevent many crimes before they escalate. No fear, no emotional reaction, no bias — just controlled action and instant reporting.
Programmed with clear legal boundaries under the Indian Penal Code and procedural limits from CrPC, they wouldn’t judge intent — only stop visible harm and alert authorities. That shifts the system from reactive justice to proactive prevention.
The goal shouldn’t be robot judges. It should be robot guardians.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@NathanXTZ you've completely missed the point.

you have to think about this from a war time industrialization perspective. boston robotics makes these dogs and robots that costs 100k each for a base model.

china is now mass producing these robots at 5k a pop. not only that, they are capable of marching longer and further without the need for repairs or maintenance.

in war time, who do you think wins? someone with advanced tech that costs millions to produce. or someone that can produce a million cheaper versions of it that is 90% as good, but extremely resilient, cost effective to manufacture and ships fast?

we've all seen the military applications of these things when they installed machine guns on top of robot dogs. none of this is new stuff.

but war, whether it's in a corporate boardroom with companies, or in real life, involves both r&d and manufacturing capabilities. yeah; boston dynamics has an extremely talented r&d team. they were the first to come up with it... but they can't scale

don't believe me, look up the prices on the boston dynamics dog. and then look up the prices of the unitree robotics dog. and you gotta ask yourself, for 20x the price, does the boston dog do anything that is THAT radically different? 

and if not, there you have your answer on why the us and china are in a trade war

snippet.textDisplay: @tinytheawesome9612  That's a fair question. First, its not going to roll out that advanced anytime soon. Right now, we still don't have AGI, we have AI. The difference is huge. The nitty gritty of industry process isn't easily replicated, much less in an efficient way.  Robots will be left doing what they are already doing which is short defined functions as you may see in an automobile assembly line.  But eventually, they will replace more and more that humans now do using software and job experience. I expect as more industry evolves, new industries will develop that will need more workers. The advent of the automobile industry put a lot of people out of jobs too, but it was so long ago, most don't realize.  Horse-drawn carts, and people cleaning up horse manure were legitimate jobs at the turn of the 20th century. As someone developing a business plan, I really want to hire human workers.  There's nothing more satisfying than being able to say to someone, "You're hired.  You start on Monday."
However, I'm doing the math, and since I'm talking about a labor-intensive manufacturing operation, the savings in labor costs by buying robotic workers is hard to deny.
I haven't made a decision yet, but I'm probably going to develop parallel plans; one that proposes human workers only, and one that makes use of robotic workers.
It'll be up to the lenders to make the call... maybe.
Really want to hire people, but the finances might not work.
Hard choice.
